findings.who: A minor or dependent adult files their own return. Their social security survivor or disability benefits are paid to a parent or other representative payee.
findings.why_no: The question asks "did you ... get social security benefits". The money went to the payee, not the filer. The help covers only the reverse case, benefits paid to you that belong to your child, so it never tells the beneficiary that benefits paid to someone else for them are theirs.
findings.irs_text: p915 p. 5, Who is taxed: "Benefits are included in the taxable income ... of the person who has the legal right to receive the benefits." ... "One-half of the part that belongs to your child must be added to your child's other income"
findings.fix: Add to the help: "Answer Yes if the benefits are yours, even if they were paid to a parent, guardian or other representative payee for you. The Form SSA-1099 is issued in your name."

findings.who: A U.S. citizen or green-card resident living abroad gets a Form SSA-1042S or RRB-1042S instead of an SSA-1099 or RRB-1099. For example, the SSA withheld tax in error because of a foreign address, or the filer never sent Form RRB-1001 to the RRB.
findings.why_no: The question says "Form SSA-1099 or Form RRB-1099 reports them", and the help keys Yes to getting a Form SSA-1099 or RRB-1099. The filer has neither form, so they read the question as not about them.
findings.irs_text: p915 p. 5: "If you are a green card holder and tax was withheld in error on your social security benefits because you have a foreign address ... you must file a Form 1040 or 1040-SR ... A copy of the Form SSA-1042S"; "If you don't file Form RRB-1001, the RRB will consider you a nonresident alien"
findings.fix: Change the gate to "... usually reported on Form SSA-1099 or RRB-1099 (or Form SSA-1042S or RRB-1042S)". Also have the gated question ask for the net benefits shown on whichever form was received.

findings.who: A retired railroad worker or a railroad survivor gets a Form RRB-1099 (tier 1 / SSEB) and a Form RRB-1099-R.
findings.why_no: The filer cannot tell whether their railroad pension counts as "railroad retirement benefits treated as social security". They think of it as a pension reported on a 1099-R, not as social security, and answer No.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 31, Lines 6a and 6b: "If you received railroad retirement benefits treated as social security, you should receive a Form RRB-1099."
findings.fix: Ask about a fact the filer can check: "Did you or your spouse get a Form RRB-1099 (the tier 1 / social security equivalent statement) from the Railroad Retirement Board?" Then explain that RRB-1099-R amounts go elsewhere.

findings.who: A U.S. resident gets only Canada Pension Plan, Quebec Pension Plan, Old Age Security or a German statutory pension, with no U.S. benefits.
findings.why_no: The question's own words name only SSA-1099 and RRB-1099 and read as U.S. social security. Only the help mentions Canada and Germany, so a filer who skips the help answers No.
findings.irs_text: p915 p. 6: "If you receive social security benefits from Canada or Germany, include them on line 1 of Worksheet 1."
findings.fix: Put Canada and Germany in the question itself: "...social security benefits (U.S., Canadian or German), or railroad retirement benefits treated as social security..."

findings.who: A retired railroad worker, or that worker's spouse on a joint return, receives tier 1 railroad retirement benefits on Form RRB-1099 and no Form SSA-1099. The 2025 payments include a retroactive amount for 2023 or 2024.
findings.why_no: The question says 'The Form SSA-1099 says so in its description of the amount in box 3.' The filer has no SSA-1099, may not think of tier 1 railroad benefits as social security, and answers no. The RRB-1099 shows prior-year amounts in its own boxes, which the question never mentions.
findings.line: ssb.lump_sum (missed refusal; the lump-sum election that could lower taxable benefits is silently forgone)
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 31, Lines 6a and 6b: 'If you received railroad retirement benefits treated as social security, you should receive a Form RRB-1099.' Line 6c: 'If any of your benefits are taxable for 2025 and they include a lump-sum benefit payment that was for an earlier year, you may be able to reduce the taxable amount with the lump-sum election.'
findings.fix: Did the 2025 social security or tier 1 railroad retirement benefits paid to you (or, on a joint return, your spouse) include a payment for an earlier year? Form SSA-1099 shows this in the description of the box 3 amount. Form RRB-1099 shows it as amounts paid in 2025 for earlier years.

findings.who: An SSDI claimant was approved in 2025 with back pay to 2023. SSA paid part of the back pay directly to the claimant's attorney as fees and withheld part to offset SSI already received. The claimant got only a small check or none.
findings.why_no: The question asks whether benefits 'paid to you' included a payment for an earlier year. The filer reads 'paid to you' as money they actually received and answers no, even though the withheld and redirected amounts count as benefits paid to them.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 31, Line 6c: 'they include a lump-sum benefit payment that was for an earlier year, you may be able to reduce the taxable amount with the lump-sum election.' Also p. 31: 'Form SSA-1099 showing in box 3 the total social security benefits paid to you.'
findings.fix: Add to the help: 'Count back pay for earlier years even if part of it went to an attorney or was withheld to repay SSI or an overpayment.'

findings.who: A disability award was decided and paid in 2025. It covers months in 2024 and 2025 and is paid as one retroactive lump sum.
findings.why_no: The filer thinks of the award as a 2025 payment because it was decided and paid in 2025. They do not read the help's pointer to the box 3 description and answer that nothing was 'for an earlier year.'
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 32, Social Security Benefits Worksheet TIP: 'If any of your benefits are taxable for 2025 and they include a lump-sum benefit payment that was for an earlier year, you may be able to reduce the taxable amount.'
findings.fix: Name the common case in the question: 'This includes back pay from a disability or retirement award that covers months before 2025.'

locators: p. 31, Line 6c; p. 32, Social Security Benefits Worksheet, TIP
